stimuli.title: Reading comprehension: memory without paper
stimuli.text:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

For most of human history, knowledge travelled without paper. Long poems, legal codes, genealogies and the rules of ritual were carried in memory and passed from teacher to student by recitation. Modern readers often assume that such a system must have been fragile, that every retelling would add errors until the original was lost. The evidence suggests otherwise. Where communities treated exact transmission as a duty, they built elaborate safeguards: texts were learnt forwards, backwards and in interlocking patterns, so that a slip in one version would be caught by the others.

These safeguards tell us something about what a community valued. A tradition that drills the precise sound of every syllable cares more about fidelity than about interpretation; the meaning may be debated, but the words may not change. A storytelling tradition, by contrast, may keep only the outline of a tale and invite each performer to colour it for the audience in front of him. Neither is a failed version of the other. They are answers to different questions about what is worth keeping.

Writing did not end oral learning so much as change its role. Once a text could be checked against a manuscript, memory was freed from the burden of storage and could turn to understanding. Yet something was lost as well. A student who has a book can postpone learning indefinitely, telling himself that the knowledge is safe on the shelf. The reciter had no such comfort: what he did not hold in mind, he did not have at all.

Today, when almost any fact can be summoned in seconds, the question returns in a new form. If storage is no longer the problem, what should a learner carry inside? The oral traditions would answer that we keep in memory whatever we expect to think with, not merely whatever we might need to look up.

stimuli.title: Reading comprehension: the shade of a street
stimuli.text:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

On a summer afternoon, two streets a few hundred metres apart can feel as if they belong to different cities. One is lined with old rain trees whose crowns meet overhead; the other is a broad road of asphalt and glass. Thermometers placed at head height on both will often differ by several degrees, and the surface of the bare road can be far hotter than the air above it. Planners have long known this, but only recently has street shade begun to be treated as public infrastructure rather than as decoration.

The change is partly a matter of measurement. When heat was described only by the city's average temperature, the shaded lane and the exposed road disappeared into a single number. Finer data, collected by sensors and by volunteers walking fixed routes, shows that heat is distributed unequally, and that the hottest streets are frequently those where people with the least choice spend their days: vendors, delivery riders and workers waiting for transport.

Trees are not a simple remedy. They need water, space for roots and years of care before they give useful shade, and a sapling planted for a ceremony and then forgotten is a gesture, not a policy. Some streets are too narrow for large crowns, and there awnings, reflective roofs and arcades may do more. The point is not that one solution fits everywhere, but that shade should be planned with the same seriousness as drains or street lights.

A city that does this well asks a modest question before it asks a grand one. Not 'how do we cool the city?', which invites slogans, but 'where does a person wait, walk and work at three in the afternoon, and what is above their head?'

stimuli.title: Reading comprehension: slow reading
stimuli.text:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

Speed is usually praised as a reading skill. Courses promise to double the number of pages a student can cover in an hour, and the habit of skimming has become so ordinary that many readers no longer notice they are doing it. Skimming has its uses. A researcher surveying a hundred abstracts to find the five that matter would be foolish to read each one slowly. The difficulty begins when a method suited to sorting is applied to understanding.

Difficult texts resist speed because their meaning is not located in single sentences. An argument may depend on a qualification made three pages earlier, or on a word used in a narrower sense than usual. The fast reader collects the conclusions and misses the conditions under which they hold. He can repeat what the author claimed but cannot say why the author believed it, and so he cannot tell when the claim stops being true.

Slow reading is not the same as reading everything slowly. It is the ability to change pace deliberately: to move quickly through familiar ground and to stop where the text becomes dense, rereading a paragraph, writing a question in the margin, or putting the argument into one's own words before going on. This is tiring, which is why it must be practised rather than merely admired.

Teachers sometimes treat a student's slowness as a weakness to be corrected. Often it is the opposite: a sign that the student has noticed something the quicker classmates passed over.

stimuli.title: Reading comprehension: the fishers' cooperative
stimuli.text:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

When the small-boat fishers of a coastal village formed a cooperative, their first aim was simple: to stop selling their catch on the beach to agents at whatever price the agents chose. By pooling the catch and renting a cold store, they could send fish to city markets themselves and bargain as a group. Within a few seasons their earnings had risen, but the cooperative had also met problems that no one had foreseen.

The first was freshness. An agent buying from one boat could refuse a poorly iced basket and move on; a cooperative selling under one name found that a single spoilt consignment harmed everyone's reputation. Fishers who had worked alone for decades now had to accept checks by their neighbours, and some resented it. The second problem was what to sell. City buyers wanted cleaned and packed fish, while many older members took pride in the sun-dried fish their families had always made.

The cooperative did not settle these problems by choosing one side. It set aside part of its income to train younger members in cleaning and packing while paying older members to teach the drying craft, and it sold the two products under different labels. Checking the ice and the catch was made a rotating duty, so that every member was at different times both the checker and the checked.

What the fishers learnt applies to many forms of collective action: shared rewards bring shared obligations, and an institution survives not by removing disagreement but by giving it a fair and regular place to be heard.

stimuli.title: Data interpretation: research scholars admitted
stimuli.text:
Study the table and answer the questions that follow.

The table shows the number of research scholars admitted by five departments of a university from 2022 to 2025.

| Department | 2022 | 2023 | 2024 | 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Botany | 24 | 30 | 27 | 36 |
| Chemistry | 42 | 38 | 45 | 51 |
| Economics | 18 | 22 | 26 | 21 |
| History | 15 | 12 | 19 | 23 |
| Physics | 33 | 36 | 39 | 42 |

stimuli.title: Data interpretation: preferred mode of learning
stimuli.text:
Study the table and answer the questions that follow.

A survey asked 2,500 adult learners which mode of learning they prefer. The table shows the number choosing each mode, by age group.

| Mode | 18 to 25 | 26 to 35 | 36 to 50 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Classroom | 240 | 180 | 210 |
| Online live | 310 | 260 | 120 |
| Recorded video | 280 | 230 | 90 |
| Blended | 170 | 230 | 180 |

stimuli.title: Data interpretation: journal articles published
stimuli.text:
Study the table and answer the questions that follow.

The table shows the number of journal articles published by the faculty of four schools of a university from 2021 to 2025.

| School | 2021 | 2022 | 2023 | 2024 | 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Arts | 14 | 17 | 21 | 19 | 26 |
| Commerce | 9 | 11 | 8 | 13 | 16 |
| Science | 37 | 41 | 44 | 52 | 49 |
| Law | 6 | 7 | 10 | 9 | 14 |

stimuli.title: Data interpretation: students by stream
stimuli.text:
Study the table and answer the questions that follow.

The table shows the 2,000 students of a college by stream and gender.

| Stream | Women | Men |
|---|---|---|
| Arts | 380 | 220 |
| Commerce | 250 | 310 |
| Science | 290 | 340 |
| Vocational | 90 | 120 |

questions.stem: At which level of teaching does the teacher aim mainly at problem solving and the learner's own critical thinking?
questions.explanation: The three levels are memory (Herbart), understanding (Morrison) and reflective (Hunt). The reflective level is problem-centred and learner-centred; the memory level aims only at retention of facts.

questions.stem: A short quiz given midway through a unit to find out what students have not yet grasped, so that teaching can be adjusted, is an example of:
questions.explanation: Formative evaluation happens during instruction to improve teaching and learning. Summative evaluation judges achievement at the end of a unit or course.

questions.stem: Which of these is a learner-centred method of teaching?
questions.explanation: In project work the learners plan, investigate and present, so they are at the centre. The lecture, dictation and teacher demonstration keep the teacher as the main actor.

questions.stem:
Consider the two statements.

Statement I: SWAYAM courses are organised in four quadrants: video lectures, reading material, self-assessment tests, and a discussion forum for doubts.

Statement II: SWAYAM Prabha delivers its educational content mainly through printed study material sent by post.

Choose the correct answer:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questions.explanation: SWAYAM's four-quadrant approach is e-tutorial (video), e-content (reading), self-assessment and a discussion forum, so Statement I is true. SWAYAM Prabha is a group of DTH television channels broadcasting educational programmes, so Statement II is false.

questions.stem: Andragogy, the study of how adults learn, holds that adult learners are most motivated when learning is:
options: free of any link to experience
relevant to problems they face now
based on rote memorisation of content
questions.explanation: Malcolm Knowles' andragogy assumes adults are self-directed, draw on their experience and are motivated by learning that solves immediate, real problems.

questions.stem: A teacher studies why her own class performs poorly in map work and tries a new method to improve it. This is:
questions.explanation: Action research is done by practitioners to solve an immediate problem in their own setting. Fundamental research aims at theory, not at a local problem.

questions.stem: A researcher divides a population into income groups and then draws a random sample from each group. This is:
questions.explanation: Stratified sampling divides the population into strata and samples randomly within each. Quota sampling also uses groups, but chooses within them non-randomly.

questions.stem: Rejecting a null hypothesis that is actually true is called:
questions.explanation: A Type I error is a false positive (rejecting a true null hypothesis); its probability is the significance level. A Type II error is failing to reject a false null hypothesis.

questions.stem: Telling participants the purpose, risks and their right to withdraw before they agree to take part is known as:
questions.explanation: Informed consent means participants agree voluntarily, knowing the purpose, procedures, risks and their right to withdraw at any time.

questions.stem: Shodhganga, run by the INFLIBNET Centre, is a repository of:
questions.explanation: Shodhganga hosts full-text PhD theses submitted by Indian universities. Shodhgangotri, its companion, holds synopses of research in progress.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the central idea of the passage?
options: Storytelling is a weaker form of learning than exact recitation
Oral traditions were unreliable until writing corrected their errors
Modern technology has made memorising knowledge unnecessary
Oral transmission could be exact, and what we memorise still matters
questions.explanation: The passage argues that oral transmission had careful safeguards and ends by asking what a learner should still carry in memory. It explicitly rejects the idea that oral systems were fragile.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why were texts learnt forwards, backwards and in interlocking patterns?
options: So that performers could vary them for each audience
So that an error in one version would be caught
So that students could finish learning them faster
So that they could later be written down accurately
questions.explanation: The last sentence of the first paragraph says these patterns meant a slip in one version would be caught by the others.

questions.stem: How does the author compare exact recitation with a storytelling tradition?
options: As an advanced and a failed form of the same practice
As traditions that ended once writing appeared
As answers to different questions about what to keep
As two methods that value interpretation equally
questions.explanation: The author says 'Neither is a failed version of the other. They are answers to different questions about what is worth keeping.'

questions.stem: What, according to the passage, did the reciter lack that a student with a book has?
options: A teacher to guide the recitation
A method of checking for errors
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says a student with a book can postpone learning, but 'the reciter had no such comfort'. The reciter did have error checks and teachers.

questions.stem: In the passage, the word 'fidelity' most nearly means:
questions.explanation: A tradition that 'cares more about fidelity than about interpretation' wants the words kept exactly as they were, that is, faithful to the original.

questions.stem: The study of how people use space and distance when they communicate is called:
questions.explanation: Proxemics (Edward T. Hall) is the use of space. Kinesics is body movement and gesture, haptics is touch and chronemics is the use of time.

questions.stem: In the Shannon and Weaver model, anything that distorts the message between sender and receiver is called:
questions.explanation: Shannon and Weaver (1949) described noise as interference in the channel. Feedback was added to the model by later writers.

questions.stem: A student misunderstands a lecture because the teacher uses the word 'significant' in its statistical sense. This is a:
questions.explanation: Semantic barriers arise from words that carry different meanings for sender and receiver. Physical barriers are noise or distance; psychological ones are emotions and attitudes.

questions.stem: The idea that the media may not tell people what to think, but do tell them what to think about, is the:
questions.explanation: Agenda-setting (McCombs and Shaw, 1972) says the media shape which issues seem important. Cultivation theory is about long-term effects of heavy television viewing on beliefs about reality.

questions.stem: In classroom communication, a student's puzzled look that makes the teacher explain again is an example of:
questions.explanation: Feedback is the receiver's response that tells the sender how the message was received. It can be verbal or non-verbal.

questions.stem: What comes next in the series 7, 11, 19, 35, 67, ?
questions.explanation: The differences double: 4, 8, 16, 32, so the next difference is 64 and 67 + 64 = 131. 99 repeats the last difference of 32.

questions.stem: What comes next in the series D, E, G, J, N, ?
questions.explanation: The gaps grow by one: D (+1) E (+2) G (+3) J (+4) N (+5) S.

questions.stem: In a certain code, TEACH is written as VGCEJ. How is LEARN written in that code?
questions.explanation: Each letter moves two places forward: L to N, E to G, A to C, R to T, N to P. MFBSO moves each letter only one place.

questions.stem: A shopkeeper marks an article 45% above its cost price and then allows a discount of 16% on the marked price. What is the profit percentage?
questions.explanation: Selling price = 1.45 x 0.84 = 1.218 times the cost, a profit of 21.8%. Subtracting 16 from 45 to get 29% ignores that the discount is taken on the higher marked price.

questions.stem: A train 264 metres long passes a signal post in 11 seconds. What is its speed?
questions.explanation: Speed = 264 / 11 = 24 m/s, and 24 x 18/5 = 86.4 km/h. 24 km/h forgets to convert from metres per second, and 39.6 converts the time instead of the speed.

questions.stem: In the classical square of opposition, 'All poets are dreamers' and 'Some poets are not dreamers' are:
questions.explanation: An A proposition and the O proposition with the same terms are contradictories: exactly one of them must be true. Contraries are A and E, which cannot both be true but can both be false.

questions.stem: 'All metals conduct electricity. Copper conducts electricity. Therefore copper is a metal.' What is wrong with this argument?
options: It has an illicit major term
questions.explanation: The middle term 'conducts electricity' is the predicate of two affirmative premises, so it is never distributed. The conclusion may be true, but it does not follow.

questions.stem: 'You cannot trust his argument for tax reform; he was once fined for parking illegally.' This is the fallacy of:
questions.explanation: Attacking the person (ad hominem) instead of the argument. The parking fine has no bearing on whether the tax argument is sound.

questions.stem: Which school of Indian philosophy accepts perception (pratyaksha) as the only valid means of knowledge?
questions.explanation: The Charvaka (Lokayata) school accepts only perception. Nyaya accepts four pramanas and Samkhya three.

questions.stem: In the inference 'The hill has fire, because it has smoke', the term 'smoke' is the:
questions.explanation: The hetu is the reason or middle term (smoke). The paksha is the subject (the hill) and the sadhya is what is to be proved (fire).

questions.stem: What was the total number of research scholars admitted by the five departments in 2024?
questions.explanation: 2024: 27 + 45 + 26 + 19 + 39 = 156. 152 comes from misreading Physics as 35.

questions.stem: Which department had the highest percentage increase in admissions from 2022 to 2025?
questions.explanation: History rose from 15 to 23, an increase of 8/15 = 53.3%. Botany rose 12/24 = 50%, Physics 9/33 = 27.3% and Chemistry 9/42 = 21.4%. Chemistry had the largest rise in numbers, not in percentage.

questions.stem: What was the average number of scholars admitted per year by the Physics department over the four years?
In how many departments did admissions rise every year from 2022 to 2025?
questions.explanation: Only Physics (33, 36, 39, 42) rose every year. Botany fell in 2024, Chemistry and History fell in 2023, and Economics fell in 2025.

questions.stem: Chemistry's share of all scholars admitted in 2025 is closest to:
questions.explanation: The 2025 total is 36 + 51 + 21 + 23 + 42 = 173, and 51 / 173 = 29.5%. 51% treats Chemistry's number as a percentage.

questions.stem: In a web address, what does 'HTTPS' stand for?
questions.explanation: HTTPS is HTTP carried over an encrypted (TLS) connection, so data between browser and server cannot easily be read in transit.

questions.stem: When sending an email, recipients in which field receive the message without the other recipients seeing their addresses?
questions.explanation: Bcc (blind carbon copy) hides those addresses from everyone else. Addresses in To and Cc are visible to all recipients.

questions.stem: A private network that uses internet technology but is open only to an organisation's own staff is an:
questions.explanation: An intranet is internal. An extranet extends controlled access to outside partners; Ethernet is a wired networking standard.

questions.stem: e-PG Pathshala, run through the INFLIBNET Centre, provides:
questions.explanation: e-PG Pathshala offers modular e-content in postgraduate subjects. Shodhganga holds theses, Vidwan is the expert database and DigiLocker stores certificates.

questions.stem: What is the decimal value of the binary number 110011?
questions.explanation: 110011 = 32 + 16 + 2 + 1 = 51. 35 drops the 16s place and 19 drops the 32s place.

questions.stem: Minamata disease, first identified in Japan, is caused by poisoning from:
questions.explanation: Minamata disease came from methylmercury in industrial waste that built up in fish. Cadmium caused itai-itai disease.

questions.stem: How many goals are there in the Sustainable Development Goals adopted by the United Nations in 2015?
questions.explanation: The 2030 Agenda has 17 goals and 169 targets. The earlier Millennium Development Goals (2000 to 2015) were 8.

questions.stem: Under India's Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016, used needles and other sharps go into a puncture-proof container of which colour?
questions.explanation: Sharps go in a white translucent puncture-proof container. Yellow is for anatomical and soiled waste, red for contaminated recyclable plastics and blue for glassware.

questions.stem:
Consider the two statements.

Statement I: The International Solar Alliance was launched by India and France at the climate conference in Paris in 2015.

Statement II: The headquarters of the International Solar Alliance is in Geneva.

Choose the correct answer:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questions.explanation: The ISA was launched at COP21 in Paris in 2015 by India and France, so Statement I is true. Its headquarters is in Gurugram, India, so Statement II is false.

questions.stem: Geothermal energy is obtained from:
questions.explanation: Geothermal energy uses heat from the Earth's interior, often where hot rock lies near the surface. Tidal energy comes from tides and biomass from plant matter.

questions.stem: The University Education Commission of 1948 to 1949, the first education commission of independent India, was chaired by:
questions.explanation: The Radhakrishnan Commission reported on university education in 1949. Mudaliar chaired the Secondary Education Commission (1952 to 1953) and Kothari the Education Commission of 1964 to 1966.

questions.stem: In which year did the University Grants Commission become a statutory body through an Act of Parliament?
questions.explanation: The UGC was set up in 1953 and became a statutory body under the UGC Act, 1956. 1953 is the year of its inauguration, not of the Act.

questions.stem: What target does the National Education Policy 2020 set for the gross enrolment ratio in higher education?
questions.explanation: NEP 2020 aims to raise the GER in higher education, including vocational education, to 50% by 2035. The 100% by 2030 target is for school education (preschool to secondary).

questions.stem: Where is the headquarters of the National Assessment and Accreditation Council (NAAC)?
questions.explanation: NAAC, set up by the UGC in 1994, is based in Bengaluru. The UGC itself is headquartered in New Delhi.

questions.stem:
Consider the two statements.

Statement I: Odantapuri was a Buddhist centre of learning in present-day Bihar.

Statement II: The ghatikas of early medieval South India were centres of learning often attached to temples.

Choose the correct answer:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questions.explanation: Odantapuri, near present-day Bihar Sharif, was a Buddhist mahavihara of the Pala period. Ghatikas, such as the one at Kanchi, were centres of Vedic and Sanskrit learning linked with temples. Both statements are true.

questions.stem: In the revised Bloom's taxonomy of the cognitive domain, which is the highest level?
questions.explanation: The revised order (Anderson and Krathwohl, 2001) is remembering, understanding, applying, analysing, evaluating and creating. In the original 1956 version, evaluation was at the top.

questions.stem: A test that reports how a student did compared with the rest of the group, rather than against a fixed standard, is:
questions.explanation: A norm-referenced test ranks a student against the group (percentiles). A criterion-referenced test compares performance with a fixed standard or mastery level.

questions.stem: Under the Choice Based Credit System, a student's overall performance across all semesters is summarised as:
questions.explanation: The SGPA (Semester Grade Point Average) covers one semester; the CGPA (Cumulative Grade Point Average) covers all semesters completed.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a learner-related factor that affects teaching?
questions.explanation: Prior knowledge belongs to the learner. Classroom size and the library are instructional facilities or institutional factors, and subject mastery is a teacher factor.

questions.stem: In a flipped classroom, students typically:
options: listen to the full lecture in class
study the lecture material before class
questions.explanation: A flipped classroom moves first exposure to content (often recorded lectures) outside class, so that class time is used for discussion, problem solving and application.

questions.stem: The positivist approach to research holds that knowledge should be based on:
questions.explanation: Positivism, associated with Auguste Comte, holds that valid knowledge comes from observable, measurable facts tested by the methods of science.

questions.stem: In an experiment on whether background music affects memory, the music is the:
questions.explanation: The researcher changes the music (independent variable) and measures memory (dependent variable).

questions.stem: In historical research, checking whether a document is genuine and not a forgery is called:
questions.explanation: External criticism tests the authenticity of a source (its date, author, material). Internal criticism tests the credibility and accuracy of what it says.

questions.stem: In a reference list, the abbreviation 'et al.' is used to:
options: shorten a list of several authors
show the source was cited earlier
questions.explanation: 'Et al.' means 'and others' and stands for the remaining authors. 'Ibid.' refers to the source cited immediately before; 'n.d.' marks no date.

questions.stem: Which of these is usually the FIRST step in the research process?
questions.explanation: Research begins by identifying and defining a problem. A review of literature then sharpens it, and hypotheses follow from the defined problem.

questions.stem: The passage is mainly concerned with:
options: proving that trees cool a city more than any roof
treating street shade as planned public infrastructure
replacing asphalt roads with narrow shaded lanes
measuring a city's average summer temperature
questions.explanation: The passage argues that shade should be planned 'with the same seriousness as drains or street lights'. It says trees are not a simple remedy, so they do not beat every alternative.

questions.stem: Why, according to the passage, did the difference between streets go unnoticed?
options: Heat was reported as one citywide average
Volunteers walked only the shaded routes
Sensors were placed too far above the road
questions.explanation: When heat was described only by the city's average temperature, the shaded lane and the exposed road 'disappeared into a single number'.

questions.stem: Which group does the passage suggest suffers most from unshaded streets?
options: Residents of streets lined with old trees
Planners who design roads and drains
People who must stay outdoors to work
questions.explanation: The hottest streets are often where 'people with the least choice spend their days: vendors, delivery riders and workers waiting for transport'.

questions.stem: What does the author say about a sapling planted for a ceremony and then forgotten?
options: It should be replaced by a reflective roof
It works better than awnings or arcades
It is the cheapest way to cool a street
It is a gesture rather than a policy
questions.explanation: The third paragraph: 'a sapling planted for a ceremony and then forgotten is a gesture, not a policy', because trees need water, space and years of care.

questions.stem: Why does the author prefer the question 'where does a person wait, walk and work at three in the afternoon?'
options: It makes the problem sound more urgent
It leads to specific, practical decisions
It can be answered with one city average
It shows that trees suit every street
questions.explanation: The broad question 'invites slogans'; the modest one points to particular places and people, so it leads to concrete action. It is the opposite of a citywide average.

questions.stem: 'Who says what in which channel to whom with what effect?' is the model of communication proposed by:
questions.explanation: Lasswell's 1948 formula gives the five questions of communication research. Berlo proposed the SMCR model; McLuhan wrote that 'the medium is the message'.

questions.stem: Tone of voice, pitch and pauses that accompany spoken words are called:
questions.explanation: Paralanguage is the vocal part of speech other than the words themselves: tone, pitch, volume, rate and pauses.

questions.stem: The two-step flow theory holds that media messages reach most people through:
questions.explanation: Lazarsfeld and Katz found that ideas flow from the media to opinion leaders and from them to others. The hypodermic needle model assumed direct and uniform effects.

questions.stem: Communication between employees at the same level in an organisation is:
questions.explanation: Horizontal (lateral) communication runs between peers. Upward goes to superiors, downward to subordinates and diagonal across both levels and departments.

questions.stem: The tendency to judge other cultures by the standards of one's own culture is called:
questions.explanation: Ethnocentrism is a barrier to intercultural communication. Cultural relativism is the opposite attitude: understanding a culture on its own terms.

questions.stem: What comes next in the series 4, 6, 12, 30, 90, ?
questions.explanation: Each term is multiplied by 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, so the next multiplier is 3.5: 90 x 3.5 = 315. 270 multiplies by 3 again.

questions.stem: Pointing to an old man, Rekha says, 'His only son is my father's father.' How is the old man related to Rekha?
questions.explanation: Rekha's father's father is her grandfather, and the old man is that grandfather's father, so he is Rekha's great-grandfather. 'Grandfather' stops one generation short.

questions.stem: The average of eight numbers is 27. If one of the numbers, 41, is removed, what is the average of the remaining seven?
questions.explanation: The eight numbers total 8 x 27 = 216. Removing 41 leaves 175, and 175 / 7 = 25.

questions.stem: What is the difference between the compound interest and the simple interest on Rs 7,500 for 2 years at 6% per annum, compounded annually?
questions.explanation: For 2 years the difference is P x (r/100)^2 = 7,500 x 0.0036 = Rs 27. 54 doubles it.

questions.stem: Two numbers are in the ratio 4 : 7. If 6 is added to each, the ratio becomes 5 : 8. What is the smaller number?
questions.explanation: Let the numbers be 4x and 7x. (4x + 6) / (7x + 6) = 5/8 gives 32x + 48 = 35x + 30, so x = 6. The numbers are 24 and 42; 30 is the smaller number after adding 6.

questions.stem: 'No reptiles are warm-blooded' is a proposition of which type?
questions.explanation: 'No S is P' is the universal negative, E. It distributes both its subject and its predicate.

questions.stem: 'Every swan I have seen in this lake is white, so the next swan I see here will probably be white.' This is:
questions.explanation: The argument generalises from observed cases to a probable conclusion, which is induction. A deductive argument's conclusion follows necessarily from its premises.

questions.stem: A valid syllogism has the mood AAA and the middle term is the subject of the major premise and the predicate of the minor premise. Its traditional name is:
questions.explanation: Barbara is AAA in the first figure (middle term: subject of the major premise, predicate of the minor). Celarent is EAE-1; Darii is AII-1; Ferio is EIO-1.

questions.stem: Knowing that a man who never eats by day but stays fat must eat at night is an example of which pramana?
questions.explanation: Arthapatti (postulation or implication) supposes a fact that alone explains an otherwise puzzling one. Upamana is knowledge by comparison; anupalabdhi is knowing an absence.

questions.stem: Author is to novel as composer is to:
questions.explanation: An author creates a novel; a composer creates a symphony. The orchestra and conductor perform it.

questions.stem: What percentage of respondents aged 36 to 50 prefer classroom learning?
questions.explanation: The 36 to 50 group has 210 + 120 + 90 + 180 = 600 respondents, and 210 / 600 = 35%. 33.3% is this group's share of all 630 classroom choosers.

questions.stem: How many respondents in all prefer online live learning?
questions.explanation: 310 + 260 + 120 = 690. The other figures are the totals for classroom, recorded video and blended.

questions.stem: Which mode of learning is preferred by the largest number of respondents overall?
questions.explanation: Totals: online live 690, classroom 630, recorded video 600, blended 580.

questions.stem: What is the ratio of respondents aged 18 to 25 who prefer recorded video to those aged 36 to 50 who prefer it?
questions.explanation: 280 : 90 = 28 : 9. 28 : 23 compares the 18 to 25 and 26 to 35 groups.

questions.stem: Respondents aged 26 to 35 who prefer blended learning form what percentage of their age group, to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: The 26 to 35 group has 180 + 260 + 230 + 230 = 900 people, and 230 / 900 = 25.6%. 39.7% is 230 out of all 580 blended choosers.

questions.stem: Which protocol is used to send email from a client to a mail server?
questions.explanation: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) sends mail. POP3 and IMAP retrieve mail from the server; FTP transfers files.

questions.stem: The system that translates a domain name such as ugc.gov.in into an IP address is the:
questions.explanation: The DNS works like a phone book for the internet, matching names to numeric addresses. A URL is the full web address itself.

questions.stem: The National Digital Library of India (NDLI) is developed by:
questions.explanation: NDLI is developed by IIT Kharagpur under the Ministry of Education's National Mission on Education through ICT. IIT Bombay runs e-Yantra and Spoken Tutorial.

questions.stem: How many bits are there in one byte?
questions.explanation: A byte is 8 bits. A nibble is 4 bits, and 1024 is the number of bytes in a kibibyte (often called a kilobyte).

questions.stem: An online service through which citizens pay property tax to a municipality is an example of:
questions.explanation: Government to Citizen (G2C) services deliver government functions directly to citizens. G2B serves businesses and G2G links government departments.

questions.stem: The Cartagena Protocol under the Convention on Biological Diversity deals with:
options: safe handling of living modified organisms
questions.explanation: The Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (2000) covers the safe transfer and use of living modified organisms. Benefit-sharing is the Nagoya Protocol; endangered species trade is CITES.

questions.stem: How many Millennium Development Goals did the United Nations set in 2000?
questions.explanation: There were 8 MDGs, for the years 2000 to 2015. They were followed by the 17 Sustainable Development Goals.

questions.stem: Itai-itai disease, which causes painful softening of the bones, is linked to:
questions.explanation: Itai-itai disease was caused by cadmium from mining waste in rice fields in Japan. Mercury caused Minamata disease.

questions.skill: National Action Plan on Climate Change
questions.stem: How many national missions did India's National Action Plan on Climate Change (2008) set out?
questions.explanation: The NAPCC launched eight national missions, including the National Solar Mission and the National Mission for Enhanced Energy Efficiency.

questions.stem: The Sendai Framework, adopted by UN member states in 2015, is concerned with:
questions.explanation: The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction runs from 2015 to 2030. Wetlands come under the Ramsar Convention and hazardous waste trade under the Basel Convention.

questions.stem: The Education Commission of 1964 to 1966, which recommended a common school system and spending 6% of national income on education, was chaired by:
questions.explanation: The Kothari Commission's report shaped the National Policy on Education of 1968. Radhakrishnan chaired the University Education Commission of 1948 to 1949.

questions.stem: Indira Gandhi National Open University, established in 1985, is an example of:
questions.explanation: IGNOU is a central open university offering programmes by distance and online learning, a non-conventional mode. It was established by an Act of Parliament, not as a deemed university.

questions.stem: Which statutory body regulates technical education, such as engineering and management, in India?
questions.explanation: The All India Council for Technical Education became statutory in 1987. NCTE regulates teacher education and NAAC accredits institutions.

questions.stem: NEP 2020 proposes four verticals under the Higher Education Commission of India. Which one would frame the expected learning outcomes, or graduate attributes, of programmes?
questions.explanation: The General Education Council sets standards and learning outcomes. The other three verticals handle funding, accreditation and regulation.

questions.stem: Which ancient centre of learning was located in present-day Gujarat?
questions.explanation: Vallabhi flourished under the Maitraka kings in Saurashtra. Odantapuri, Vikramashila and Nalanda were in present-day Bihar.

questions.stem: Teaching is best described as:
options: an interaction that helps others learn
the reading of prescribed texts aloud
a one-way transfer of information to pupils
the setting and marking of tests
questions.explanation: Modern definitions treat teaching as an interactive process aimed at bringing about learning. Transmission of information is only one part of it.

questions.stem: The memory level of teaching is associated with:
questions.explanation: Herbart is associated with the memory level, Morrison with the understanding level and Hunt with the reflective level.

questions.stem: At the understanding level of teaching, the main aim is for learners to:
options: pose and solve their own problems
questions.explanation: The understanding level (Morrison) goes beyond memory to the meaning of facts, their relationships and generalisations. Posing and solving problems belongs to the reflective level.

questions.stem: A test given before a course begins to decide which group or level a student should join is:
questions.explanation: Placement evaluation decides where to start or which section to join. Diagnostic evaluation looks for the causes of persistent learning difficulties.

questions.stem: Diagnostic evaluation is mainly used to:
options: find the causes of a learning difficulty
decide the length of a syllabus
certify that a course is complete
questions.explanation: Diagnostic tests identify specific weaknesses and their causes, so that remedial teaching can address them.

questions.stem: A test that measures what it is meant to measure is said to have high:
questions.explanation: Validity is measuring the right thing. Reliability is giving consistent results; a test can be reliable without being valid.

questions.stem: Which characteristic of adolescent learners should a teacher keep in mind most?
options: A strong need for peer acceptance
A lack of interest in identity
questions.explanation: Adolescence brings a strong orientation to peers and the search for identity. Adolescents can usually think abstractly (Piaget's formal operations).

questions.stem: Which of these is an ICT-based teaching support system?
questions.explanation: A learning management system (such as Moodle) is ICT-based. The chalkboard, chart and flannel board are traditional aids.

questions.stem:
Consider the two statements.

Statement I: In computer adaptive testing, every candidate must answer the same set of questions in the same order.

Statement II: In computer adaptive testing, the difficulty of the next question depends on the candidate's answers so far.

Choose the correct answer:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questions.explanation: An adaptive test chooses each next item from the candidate's performance, so candidates see different sets. Statement I is false and Statement II is true.

questions.stem: The seminar method of teaching is most suitable for:
questions.explanation: In a seminar, a learner presents a paper and others discuss it critically. It suits postgraduate and research students.

questions.stem: Which method of teaching is based on dividing learning into small steps with immediate feedback after each?
questions.explanation: Programmed instruction, based on B. F. Skinner's operant conditioning, presents material in small frames and reinforces each correct response immediately.

questions.stem: Which of these is a basic requirement of effective teaching?
questions.explanation: Effective teaching starts from clear objectives that guide the choice of methods and assessment. Questions and interaction help learning rather than hinder it.

questions.stem: Research carried out mainly to develop or extend a theory, without an immediate practical use, is:
questions.explanation: Fundamental (basic or pure) research aims at knowledge and theory; applied research uses knowledge to solve a practical problem.

questions.stem: Which of these is a non-probability sampling method?
questions.explanation: In purposive (judgement) sampling the researcher chooses cases deliberately. Random, systematic and cluster sampling give every unit a known chance of selection.

questions.stem: A researcher studying a hidden population asks each person interviewed to suggest others to contact. This is:
questions.explanation: Snowball (chain referral) sampling grows through referrals and suits hard-to-reach groups.

questions.stem: Which of these is a typical method of qualitative research?
questions.explanation: Qualitative research seeks meanings and experiences through in-depth interviews, observation and documents. Surveys, trials and tests produce quantitative data.

questions.stem: A hypothesis stating that there is no relationship between two variables is a:
questions.explanation: The null hypothesis (H0) states no effect or no relationship; the study tests whether the data allow it to be rejected.

questions.stem: A study that records how many hours undergraduates spend online each day, without changing anything, is:
questions.explanation: Descriptive research describes a situation as it exists. Experimental and quasi-experimental designs manipulate a variable.

questions.stem: Post-positivism differs from positivism mainly in accepting that:
options: facts cannot be measured at all
all observation is fallible and theory-laden
questions.explanation: Post-positivists keep the scientific method but hold that knowledge is provisional and that observation is shaped by theory and error.

questions.stem: The APA style of referencing cites a source in the text by:
questions.explanation: APA uses author-date citations, such as (Rao, 2019). MLA uses author and page, and some styles use numbered notes.

questions.stem: Presenting another person's work or ideas as one's own is:
questions.explanation: Plagiarism is using another's words or ideas without credit. Fabrication is inventing data; falsification is altering data or results.

questions.stem: Under the UGC's 2018 regulations on academic integrity, a similarity level of up to 10% in a thesis is:
options: a ground for withdrawing the thesis
treated as minor, with no penalty
a ground for cancelling the degree
treated as the most serious level
questions.explanation: The UGC (Promotion of Academic Integrity and Prevention of Plagiarism in Higher Educational Institutions) Regulations, 2018 treat similarity up to 10% as Level 0, a minor similarity with no penalty. Higher levels carry graded penalties.

questions.stem: A researcher has an h-index of 7. This means the researcher has:
options: 7 papers each cited at least 7 times
questions.explanation: The h-index is the largest h such that h of the researcher's papers have at least h citations each.

questions.stem: In a thesis, the chapter that relates the findings to earlier studies and explains what they mean is usually the:
questions.explanation: The discussion interprets the results and connects them with the literature. The methodology chapter describes how the study was done.

questions.stem: The author's main argument is that:
options: reading speed courses help with difficult texts
good readers change pace to suit the text
every text should be read as slowly as possible
skimming should never be used in research
questions.explanation: The third paragraph defines slow reading as 'the ability to change pace deliberately'. The author accepts skimming for sorting and rejects reading everything slowly.

questions.stem: For which task does the author say skimming is appropriate?
options: Sorting many abstracts to find a few
Spotting a word used in a narrow sense
Learning why an author holds a view
questions.explanation: The first paragraph: a researcher surveying a hundred abstracts to find the five that matter would be foolish to read each slowly.

questions.stem: Why, according to the passage, can the fast reader not tell when a claim stops being true?
options: He did not remember the author's conclusion
He wrote too many questions in the margin
He missed the conditions on which it rests
He read the qualification too many times
questions.explanation: The fast reader 'collects the conclusions and misses the conditions under which they hold', so he cannot see where a claim's limits are.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT given in the passage as a practice of slow reading?
options: Reading every page at one steady pace
Writing a question in the margin
Restating the argument in one's own words
questions.explanation: The passage says slow reading 'is not the same as reading everything slowly'; the other three are listed as ways to stop where the text becomes dense.

questions.stem: The author's attitude to a student who reads slowly is best described as:
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says slowness is often 'a sign that the student has noticed something' others missed, a sympathetic view.

questions.stem: What was the cooperative's first aim?
options: To train young fishers in packing
To check the freshness of every basket
To revive the making of dried fish
To stop selling the catch to agents
questions.explanation: The first paragraph: their first aim was 'to stop selling their catch on the beach to agents at whatever price the agents chose'.

questions.stem: Why did freshness become a shared problem once the fishers sold together?
options: City buyers refused all sun-dried fish
One spoilt batch harmed every member's name
Older members would not use the cold store
questions.explanation: Selling 'under one name', a single spoilt consignment 'harmed everyone's reputation'.

questions.stem: How did the cooperative handle the disagreement over what to sell?
options: It switched entirely to cleaned, packed fish
It stopped paying the older members
It let the city buyers set every price
It sold both products under separate labels
questions.explanation: It trained younger members in cleaning and packing, paid older members to teach drying and sold the two products under different labels.

questions.stem: Making the checks a rotating duty was meant mainly to:
options: hand quality control back to the agents
make checking feel fair to every member
let the best fishers avoid inspection
reduce the amount of fish to be checked
questions.explanation: Each member was at different times 'both the checker and the checked', which spreads the burden fairly and answers the resentment the passage mentions.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the lesson of the passage?
options: Agents are needed for any fishery to survive
Cooperatives succeed by removing all disagreement
Traditional products always sell better in cities
questions.explanation: The last paragraph: 'shared rewards bring shared obligations', and institutions survive by giving disagreement a fair place, not by removing it.

questions.stem: Converting an idea into words, symbols or signals to send it is called:
questions.explanation: The sender encodes; the receiver decodes the message back into meaning.

questions.stem: Gestures, posture and facial expressions are studied under:
questions.explanation: Kinesics, a term from Ray Birdwhistell, is the study of body movement as communication.

questions.stem: Arriving late to a meeting can send a message about respect. This aspect of non-verbal communication is:
questions.explanation: Chronemics is the use and perception of time in communication: punctuality, waiting and the pace of speech.

questions.stem: Informal communication that spreads through personal networks in an organisation is called the:
questions.explanation: The grapevine is the informal network. It is fast but may carry rumour.

questions.stem: In group communication, the tendency of members to agree in order to avoid conflict, at the cost of good decisions, is called:
questions.explanation: Groupthink (Irving Janis) occurs when the desire for harmony suppresses critical evaluation of alternatives.

questions.stem: Cultivation theory, developed by George Gerbner, is concerned with:
options: how opinion leaders pass on messages
how heavy TV viewing shapes beliefs about reality
how editors decide which stories to publish
questions.explanation: Gerbner found heavy viewers tend to see the real world as more like the world shown on television. Choosing stories is gatekeeping; choosing media is uses and gratifications.

questions.stem: The process by which editors decide which news items reach the audience is called:
questions.explanation: Gatekeeping, from Kurt Lewin and applied to news by David Manning White, describes the selection and filtering of news.

questions.stem: The uses and gratifications approach assumes that audiences:
options: receive identical effects from a message
actively choose media to meet their needs
questions.explanation: Uses and gratifications (Blumler and Katz) treats the audience as active, choosing media for information, entertainment, identity or social contact.

questions.stem: The spiral of silence theory says that people are less likely to voice an opinion when they:
options: hear it from an opinion leader
have read about it in a newspaper
share it with a large majority
believe it is a minority view
questions.explanation: Elisabeth Noelle-Neumann argued that fear of isolation makes people who think they hold a minority view stay silent, so the majority view seems stronger still.

questions.stem: Which of these makes classroom communication most effective?
options: Speaking quickly to cover the whole syllabus
Using as much jargon as possible
questions.explanation: Questions give the teacher feedback and keep learners engaged. Speed, jargon and lack of eye contact are barriers.

questions.stem: 'The medium is the message' is a statement by:
questions.explanation: McLuhan (1964) argued that the form of a medium shapes society as much as its content. He also coined 'the global village'.

questions.stem:
Consider the two statements.

Statement I: Non-verbal cues can contradict the spoken words of a message.

Statement II: Non-verbal communication carries the same meaning in every culture.

Choose the correct answer:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questions.explanation: A smile with a sharp tone, for example, can contradict the words, so Statement I is true. Gestures and eye contact mean different things in different cultures, so Statement II is false.

questions.stem: Which of these fractions is the largest?
The price of a book rises by 15% and then by a further 20%. What is the overall increase?
questions.explanation: 1.15 x 1.20 = 1.38, so the overall rise is 38%. Adding 15 and 20 to get 35% ignores that the second rise applies to the already higher price.

questions.stem: A cyclist rides the first half of a journey at 12 km/h and the second half, of equal length, at 18 km/h. What is the average speed for the whole journey?
questions.explanation: For equal distances the average speed is 2ab / (a + b) = 2 x 12 x 18 / 30 = 14.4 km/h. 15 km/h is the simple average of the speeds, which would be right only for equal times.

questions.stem: Two successive discounts of 12% and 5% are equal to a single discount of:
questions.explanation: A customer pays 0.88 x 0.95 = 0.836 of the price, so the single discount is 16.4%. Adding them to get 17% counts the second discount on the full price.

questions.stem: The simple interest on a sum for 4 years at 7.5% per annum is Rs 1,560. What is the sum?
In a code, A is written as Z, B as Y, C as X and so on. How is DATA written?
questions.explanation: Each letter is replaced by its mirror in the alphabet: D to W, A to Z, T to G, A to Z.

questions.stem: What comes next in the series AZ, CX, FU, JQ, ?
questions.explanation: First letters move +2, +3, +4, +5: A, C, F, J, O. Second letters move -2, -3, -4, -5: Z, X, U, Q, L.

questions.stem: What comes next in the series 4, 11, 30, 67, 128, ?
questions.explanation: Each term is n cubed plus 3: 1 + 3, 8 + 3, 27 + 3, 64 + 3, 125 + 3, so the next is 216 + 3 = 219. 217 adds only 1 to 216, and 190 adds the last difference (61) again.

questions.stem: P is Q's sister. R is the only brother of P's mother. How is Q related to R?
questions.explanation: R is the brother of Q's mother, so R is Q's maternal uncle and Q is R's nephew or niece. Q's sex is not given, so 'nephew' alone cannot be concluded.

questions.stem: Rs 9,450 is divided among P, Q and R in the ratio 3 : 5 : 7. What is R's share?
questions.explanation: R gets 7/15 of 9,450 = Rs 4,410. 1,890 is P's share and 3,150 is Q's.

questions.stem: The average age of 35 trainees is 16 years. When the instructor's age is included, the average rises by half a year. How old is the instructor?
questions.explanation: The 36 people total 36 x 16.5 = 594 years, and the trainees total 35 x 16 = 560, so the instructor is 34. 16.5 is only the new average.

questions.stem: By selling an article for Rs 1,173, a trader makes a profit of 15%. What was the cost price?
questions.explanation: Cost = 1,173 / 1.15 = Rs 1,020. 997 subtracts 15% of the selling price instead.

questions.stem: If 'Some books are costly' is false, what can be said of 'No books are costly'?
questions.explanation: I and E propositions with the same terms are contradictories, so if the I is false, the E must be true.

questions.stem: Which pair of propositions can both be true but cannot both be false?
questions.explanation: I and O are subcontraries: at least one is true. A and E are contraries; A and O, and E and I, are contradictories.

questions.stem: In the proposition 'Some students are not athletes', which term is distributed?
questions.explanation: An O proposition distributes its predicate only: it says something about every athlete, namely that the students in question are excluded from that whole class.

questions.stem: The set of objects to which a term applies is called its:
questions.explanation: Denotation (extension) is the class of things a term refers to. Connotation (intension) is the set of qualities the term implies.

questions.stem: 'God exists because the scriptures say so, and the scriptures are true because they are the word of God.' This commits the fallacy of:
questions.explanation: The conclusion is assumed in a premise, so the argument goes in a circle (petitio principii).

questions.stem: 'Since the new principal joined, exam results have fallen. Her arrival must have caused it.' This is the fallacy of:
questions.explanation: Assuming that because one event came after another it was caused by it (post hoc ergo propter hoc).

questions.stem: Premises: All sailors are swimmers. Some swimmers are coaches. Which conclusion follows?
options: Neither 'some sailors are coaches' nor its denial
questions.explanation: A Venn diagram can place the coaching swimmers entirely outside the sailors, or partly inside, so nothing definite follows about sailors and coaches.

questions.stem: How many pramanas does the Nyaya school accept?
questions.explanation: Nyaya accepts perception, inference, comparison (upamana) and verbal testimony (shabda). Buddhist logicians accept two; Samkhya three; Bhatta Mimamsa and Advaita Vedanta six.

questions.stem: Knowing that there is no pot on the floor simply by not perceiving one there is, for the Bhatta Mimamsa school, the pramana of:
questions.explanation: Anupalabdhi (non-apprehension) is the means of knowing absence, accepted as a separate pramana by Kumarila's Bhatta Mimamsa and by Advaita Vedanta.

questions.stem: In Nyaya, a reason (hetu) that is found with both the presence and the absence of what is to be proved is the fallacy called:
questions.explanation: Savyabhichara is the 'irregular' or inconclusive reason. Viruddha proves the opposite; asiddha is an unproved reason; badhita is contradicted by a stronger pramana.

questions.stem: In Indian logic, vyapti refers to:
options: knowledge gained from a trustworthy word
a fallacy of an unproved reason
the invariable relation of hetu and sadhya
the subject in which a property is inferred
questions.explanation: Vyapti is the universal, invariable concomitance between the reason and what is to be proved, such as 'wherever there is smoke there is fire'. The subject is the paksha.

questions.stem: 'Please close the door' serves which function of language?
questions.explanation: A request or command directs action. Informative language states facts; expressive language conveys feeling.

questions.stem: How many articles did the four schools publish in 2023?
What was the average number of articles per year published by the School of Science?
In which year was the increase in the total number of articles over the previous year the largest?
questions.explanation: Totals: 66, 76, 83, 93, 105. Increases: 10, 7, 10, 12, so 2025 had the largest rise.

questions.stem: By what percentage did the School of Commerce's output rise from 2021 to 2025?
questions.explanation: From 9 to 16 is a rise of 7, and 7 / 9 = 77.8%. 43.8% divides by the new value (7 / 16); 177.8% is the new value as a percentage of the old.

questions.stem: The School of Arts' share of all articles over the five years is closest to:
What is the ratio of women to men in the Arts stream?
questions.explanation: 380 : 220 = 19 : 11 (dividing both by 20).

questions.stem: Women form roughly what percentage of the Science stream?
questions.explanation: Science has 290 + 340 = 630 students, and 290 / 630 = 46.0%. 54% is the share of men.

questions.stem: In which stream do women make up the largest share of the stream's students?
questions.explanation: Women's shares: Arts 380/600 = 63.3%, Science 290/630 = 46.0%, Commerce 250/560 = 44.6%, Vocational 90/210 = 42.9%.

questions.stem: If the four stream totals were shown on a pie chart, what would be the central angle, in degrees, for Commerce?
questions.explanation: Commerce has 250 + 310 = 560 of 2,000 students, and 560 / 2000 x 360 = 100.8 degrees. 113.4 is the angle for Science (630).

questions.stem: Taking Commerce and Vocational together, how many more men are there than women?
questions.explanation: Men: 310 + 120 = 430. Women: 250 + 90 = 340. 430 - 340 = 90. 60 is the Commerce gap alone, 30 the Vocational gap.

questions.stem: What does 'MOOC' stand for?
questions.explanation: A MOOC is an online course open to very large numbers of learners, such as the courses offered on SWAYAM.

questions.stem: VoIP is a technology for:
options: encrypting files on a hard disk
questions.explanation: Voice over Internet Protocol carries voice calls as data packets over IP networks.

questions.stem: A network that connects computers within a single building or campus is a:
questions.explanation: A local area network covers a building or campus. A MAN covers a city and a WAN spans countries; a PAN links one person's devices.

questions.stem: Which protocol keeps emails on the server and synchronises them across several devices?
questions.explanation: IMAP leaves mail on the server so every device sees the same folders. POP3 usually downloads and removes it.

questions.stem: A webinar is best described as:
options: a seminar conducted over the internet
a recorded lecture on a disc
an email sent to many people
questions.explanation: A webinar (web seminar) is a live online presentation in which participants can usually ask questions or chat.

questions.stem: What is the binary form of the decimal number 54?
questions.explanation: 54 = 32 + 16 + 4 + 2, which is 110110 in binary.

questions.stem: NPTEL, which offers online courses in engineering and science, is a joint initiative of:
questions.explanation: The National Programme on Technology Enhanced Learning was started by seven IITs and IISc Bengaluru and is a national coordinator for SWAYAM engineering courses.

questions.stem: The Academic Bank of Credits allows a student to:
options: store credits earned and use them later
questions.explanation: The Academic Bank of Credits, introduced under NEP 2020, keeps a digital record of credits earned at registered institutions, enabling multiple entry and exit and credit transfer.

questions.stem: Degree certificates and mark sheets issued in digital form to students are stored in the:
questions.explanation: The National Academic Depository, accessed through DigiLocker, is an online store of academic awards. The National Knowledge Network is a high-speed research network.

questions.stem: Software whose source code is freely available to use, study and modify is called:
questions.explanation: Open-source licences allow anyone to read and change the code. Shareware is free to try but closed; firmware is software built into hardware.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of a web browser?
questions.explanation: Firefox is a browser. Excel is a spreadsheet, Photoshop an image editor and Linux an operating system kernel.

questions.stem: A department wants to be able to recover its research data if a ransomware attack encrypts its computers. Which measure helps most?
options: Copying files to a shared network drive
questions.explanation: Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment to unlock them. A recent backup kept offline, where the malware cannot reach it, lets the data be restored without paying. A shared network drive is still connected, so ransomware can encrypt it too; zipping or renaming files does not protect them.

questions.stem: The Nagoya Protocol under the Convention on Biological Diversity concerns:
options: access to genetic resources and benefit-sharing
safe transfer of living modified organisms
questions.explanation: The Nagoya Protocol (2010) covers access to genetic resources and the fair sharing of benefits from their use. The Cartagena Protocol is about living modified organisms.

questions.stem: Which document was adopted at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit?
questions.explanation: The Rio Summit adopted Agenda 21 and the Rio Declaration, and opened the climate change and biodiversity conventions for signature. The Kyoto Protocol came in 1997.

questions.stem: Blue baby syndrome in infants is linked to excess of which substance in drinking water?
questions.explanation: High nitrate levels reduce the blood's ability to carry oxygen in infants (methaemoglobinaemia). Excess fluoride causes fluorosis.

questions.stem: Excess fluoride in drinking water over many years causes:
questions.explanation: Fluorosis damages teeth and bones. Goitre is linked to iodine deficiency and rickets to vitamin D deficiency.

questions.stem: Acid rain is caused mainly by emissions of:
questions.explanation: Sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides form sulphuric and nitric acids in the atmosphere, which fall as acid rain.

questions.stem: Which renewable energy source comes from solar energy stored by plants and other organic matter?
questions.explanation: Biomass (wood, crop residues, dung) stores energy captured by photosynthesis. Geothermal energy is the Earth's internal heat and tidal energy comes mainly from the Moon's pull.

questions.stem: Old cathode ray tube (CRT) monitors are hazardous e-waste mainly because their glass contains:
questions.explanation: CRT glass contains a large amount of lead to shield users from radiation, which makes careless disposal dangerous.

questions.stem: Under India's Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000, the area within 100 metres of hospitals, schools and courts is a:
questions.explanation: The rules declare an area of at least 100 metres around hospitals, educational institutions and courts a silence zone, with the lowest permitted noise levels.

questions.stem: Excessive growth of algae in a lake caused by fertiliser run-off is called:
questions.explanation: Nitrates and phosphates from fertilisers feed algal blooms, which use up oxygen when they decay. Biomagnification is the build-up of a toxin along a food chain.

questions.stem: Which of these is a structural measure for mitigating floods?
questions.explanation: Structural measures are physical constructions such as embankments and dams. Warnings, awareness and zoning are non-structural measures.

questions.stem: PM2.5 refers to:
options: gases present at 2.5 parts per million
questions.explanation: PM2.5 is fine particulate matter with a diameter of 2.5 micrometres or less, small enough to reach deep into the lungs.

questions.stem:
Consider the two statements.

Statement I: A wind turbine converts the kinetic energy of moving air into electricity.

Statement II: Solar photovoltaic cells convert sunlight directly into electricity.

Choose the correct answer:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questions.explanation: Both statements describe how these renewable sources work, so both are true.

questions.stem: The National Institutional Ranking Framework (NIRF) is used to:
questions.explanation: NIRF, launched by the Ministry of Education in 2015, ranks institutions on parameters such as teaching, research, outcomes, outreach and perception.

questions.stem: Rashtriya Uchchatar Shiksha Abhiyan (RUSA), launched in 2013, mainly funds:
questions.explanation: RUSA is a centrally sponsored scheme to improve access, equity and quality in state universities and colleges.

questions.stem: Under which section of the UGC Act, 1956, can an institution be declared a deemed-to-be university?
questions.explanation: Section 3 allows the central government, on UGC advice, to declare an institution deemed to be a university. Section 2(f) defines a university, and 12B covers eligibility for UGC grants.

questions.stem: How many levels does India's National Skills Qualifications Framework (NSQF) have?
questions.explanation: The NSQF organises qualifications into 10 levels by the knowledge, skills and responsibility each requires.

questions.stem: A pathshala teaching Sanskrit texts or a madrasa teaching Arabic and Persian texts is an example of:
questions.explanation: Oriental learning refers to traditional institutions teaching classical Indian and Islamic languages and texts.

questions.stem: Environmental education was made compulsory at every level of education following a Supreme Court case filed by:
questions.explanation: In M. C. Mehta v. Union of India (1991), the Supreme Court directed that environmental education be taught at all levels, and the UGC later introduced a compulsory undergraduate course.

questions.stem: Under NEP 2020's multiple exit options, a student who leaves a bachelor's programme after completing two years receives a:
questions.explanation: The policy awards a certificate after one year, a diploma after two years, a bachelor's degree after three, and a bachelor's degree with research after four.

questions.stem: A central university in India is established by:
options: an Act of a state legislature
questions.explanation: Central universities are created by Acts of Parliament, and state universities by Acts of state legislatures.

questions.stem: The main aim of value education is to:
questions.explanation: Value education helps learners develop moral judgement, respect for others and responsible citizenship.

questions.stem: The National Policy on Education of 1986 was modified, with a new Programme of Action, in:
questions.explanation: The 1986 policy was modified in 1992 after reviews by the Acharya Ramamurti Committee (1990) and a CABE committee chaired by N. Janardhana Reddy (1991), and a revised Programme of Action followed the same year.

questions.stem: The main function of NAAC is to:
questions.explanation: NAAC assesses and accredits higher education institutions. The UGC gives grants, the NTA conducts the UGC-NET and the AICTE approves technical institutions.

questions.stem: The Indian Institutes of Technology have the status of:
questions.explanation: IITs are Institutes of National Importance under the Institutes of Technology Act, 1961, which gives them the power to award their own degrees.
